clue.text: Tree shelters hares running, something not usually experienced indoors

indicators.note: to shelter something is to hold it inside, so one word goes round the other
creatures running scatter about, so the letters beside this word are jumbled

blocks.note: a fir is a conifer
taken as written, then jumbled

explanation.surface: Hares dash for cover under a tree, out in the open countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Running' looks like what the hares are doing; it tells you to jumble them.
explanation.definitionFit: Outdoor atmosphere, breathed outside rather than in a room, is what people mean by going out for this.

clue.text: Man doubles on the drum

blocks.note: Tom is a man's name
the man's name is written a second time

explanation.surface: A man plays two parts in a band, doubling up on the drum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doubles on the drum' sounds like a percussionist's job; here 'doubles' just says to write the name twice.
explanation.definitionFit: A tom-tom is a tall, narrow percussion instrument beaten with the hands or sticks.

clue.text: A crossword person, I gather

definitions.note: the clue speaks as the person, a self-description rather than a noun

blocks.note: first meaning: the setter who writes a puzzle
second meaning: one who collects things together, speaking in the first person

explanation.walkthrough: 'I gather' reads as 'I believe' but is the setter speaking: someone who gathers material is one who compiles it.
explanation.definitionFit: Puzzle setters are traditionally called compilers, and to compile literally means to gather and assemble material.

clue.text: Refrain that's difficult to bear

blocks.note: first meaning: the chorus repeated in a song
second meaning: a heavy load or hardship

explanation.surface: A tune's chorus so annoying it becomes unbearable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refrain' looks like a verb meaning hold back; it is the noun, a song's chorus, an old sense of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavy load is something hard to carry, and the archaic musical term for a recurring chorus shares the spelling.

clue.text: Dog upset tailless zoo bird

indicators.note: without a tail, the final letter is cut from each of the following words
things upset are knocked into disorder, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
a robin is a common garden bird

explanation.surface: A dog upsets a bird at the zoo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tailless' docks both words, leaving ZO and ROBI to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The borzoi is a tall Russian breed of hound, once used for hunting wolves.

clue.text: Stump with device to retrain the flow

blocks.note: first meaning: to puzzle or perplex
second meaning: a plate or screen that restrains or redirects a flow of fluid or sound

explanation.surface: A tree stump fitted with a contraption to redirect a stream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stump' looks like a noun, a tree remnant; it is the verb meaning to puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: To stump someone is to perplex them, and engineers fit plates of this name to check or divert currents.

clue.text: Strong old boy in sign of deterioration

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: corrosion on metal shows decay
OB is the abbreviation for old boy, a former pupil

explanation.surface: A former pupil, once strong, is now showing his age.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something sturdy, healthy and able to withstand pressure: close synonyms.

clue.text: Naughty child with hard problem losing its head

indicators.note: a word that loses its head has its first letter removed

blocks.note: first meaning: a mischievous youngster
a stinker is a very difficult question or task

explanation.surface: A parent struggles with a badly behaved child, a real problem.
explanation.walkthrough: STINKER without its first letter gives a second route to TINKER.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling a mischievous youngster a little tinker is an affectionate British idiom for a scamp.

clue.text: Repeat rides around temporary dwellings

indicators.note: letters turned around are moved out of place and reordered

blocks.note: taken as written, then jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone keeps repeating journeys between temporary homes.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural is needed: REPEAT RIDES has an S and one A, and the enumeration (5-1-5) fits PIEDS-A-TERRE, not the printed key.
explanation.definitionFit: These French-borrowed terms name small flats or rooms kept for occasional stays away from one's main home.

clue.text: Kind of printing no longer available to produce

blocks.note: a dish that is off is no longer on the menu
plants set fruit or seed when they produce it

explanation.surface: A printing method that has gone out of production.
explanation.definitionFit: Offset lithography transfers an inked image to a rubber blanket and then onto paper, a common commercial process.

clue.text: Unwise, not right, impolite

indicators.note: 'not' with right means the letter standing for right is taken away

blocks.note: imprudent means lacking good sense

explanation.surface: A list of three faults: foolish, wrong and rude.
explanation.walkthrough: R is the standard abbreviation for right; removing it from IMPRUDENT leaves IMPUDENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Impudent describes cheeky, disrespectful behaviour, a close synonym for rude or discourteous.

clue.text: Appropriate part of school game for a girl

indicators.note: to appropriate is to take, so a section is lifted out of the following words

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A suitable school sport for a girl to play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appropriate' looks like an adjective meaning suitable; it is the verb meaning take.
explanation.definitionFit: Olga is a Russian female given name, so it is one example of a name for a girl.

clue.text: One to discredit Nigel's drum playing

indicators.note: playing about with something moves it around freely, so the letters are reordered

blocks.note: taken as written, then jumbled

explanation.surface: A critic sets out to rubbish Nigel's drumming.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who throws dirt figuratively, making malicious accusations to damage a rival's reputation, especially in politics.

clue.text: A way round the conurbation ...

blocks.note: surface reading: a method of getting around a city
setter's reading: literally a route encircling the urban area, a ring road

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links this to the clue at 18, which offers a route through the town instead of round it.
explanation.definitionFit: A ring road circling a city, letting traffic bypass the centre, is what this British term names.

clue.text: Where the crisps are secure

blocks.note: first meaning: the literal location of packet snacks
second meaning: certain to be won, as good as achieved

explanation.walkthrough: Crisps are what Americans call potato chips, sold in packets; the idiom means a result is certain.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a victory or outcome already assured, as if captured and tied up safely.

clue.text: Exhausted colleague's year off taking everything together

indicators.note: off means removed, so the letter for year is dropped

blocks.note: all in is a colloquial phrase for worn out
an ally is a partner or associate

explanation.surface: A tired coworker takes a gap year after all.
explanation.walkthrough: Y is the abbreviation for year, removed from ALLY.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means considering every factor at once, overall, on balance.

clue.text: Garment I'm acting in turned up all right

indicators.note: in a down entry something turned up is read from the bottom upwards
one thing placed in another sits inside it

blocks.note: OK is shorthand for all right
taken as written
a performer who is on is on stage

explanation.surface: An actor says the costume they're performing in turned out fine.
explanation.definitionFit: A kimono is a long, wide-sleeved Japanese robe tied with a sash.

clue.text: Fawn is an animal, say, to draw

indicators.note: say means as spoken, so the word is written as it sounds rather than as spelt

blocks.note: a cow is a farm animal
to tow is to pull along

explanation.surface: A young deer described as an animal someone might sketch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fawn' looks like a young deer, which fits 'animal'; it is the verb meaning grovel.
explanation.definitionFit: To fawn is to flatter servilely, and to kowtow, from the Chinese ritual of kneeling, means to act submissively.

clue.text: ... or a way though it

blocks.note: surface reading: an alternative route, continuing the previous clue about the city
setter's reading: the main street running through the middle of a town

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis continues 13 across: 'it' is the conurbation, and 'though' stands for 'through'. In Britain this is the usual name for a town's main shopping street.
explanation.definitionFit: A town's principal road, lined with shops, passes through its centre rather than around it.

clue.text: In confusion, I had run out Bob

indicators.note: something in confusion is muddled, so the letters are mixed up

blocks.note: taken as written
ro is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for run out

explanation.surface: A batsman named Bob, flustered, admits he was run out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bob' looks like a name; it is the short haircut.
explanation.definitionFit: A bob is a short haircut cut level around the head, one particular style of arranging the hair.

clue.text: Paddy's mood

blocks.note: first meaning: a fit of anger, a tantrum
second meaning: state of mind or disposition

explanation.walkthrough: Paddy looks like a man's name (often an Irishman's); in British English a paddy is a fit of temper.
explanation.definitionFit: Losing one's rag is a burst of anger, and a person's disposition or frame of mind shares this name.

clue.text: Ring Kitty back

indicators.note: going back means travelling the opposite way, so the word is read right to left

blocks.note: a kitty is a shared fund of money

explanation.surface: Telephone the cat to come home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kitty' suggests a cat; here it is a pot of money.
explanation.definitionFit: A circular shape or band made by a curve closing on itself is a loop, much as a ring is.

clue.text: Actor holding the pit can act with arrogance

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it within, so one piece wraps round another

blocks.note: a doer is one who acts
a mine is a coal pit

explanation.surface: A performer in the orchestra pit behaves arrogantly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Actor' suggests the stage; it means simply one who acts.
explanation.definitionFit: To domineer is to assert one's will over others in an overbearing, imperious manner.

clue.text: Detailed short note seen in time

blocks.note: first meaning: tiny, precise in every particular
second meaning: a brief written memorandum

explanation.surface: A precise memo arrives promptly.
explanation.walkthrough: Pronounced differently, the word is an adjective for precise and a noun for a memo; 'time' hints at a third sense, sixty seconds.
explanation.definitionFit: A careful, exhaustive inspection is called minute, and a brief official record or memorandum shares the spelling.

clue.text: Test limits of dependence in examination

indicators.note: the limits of a word are its boundaries, so only its first and last letters are kept
one thing placed in another sits inside it

blocks.note: an oral is a spoken exam
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A test that measures how far someone relies on others.
explanation.definitionFit: A severe trial or painful experience that tests endurance; historically, a trial by fire or water.

clue.text: Chap to produce knock down, followed by a cry of pain

blocks.note: to fell is to strike down
ow is an exclamation of hurt

explanation.surface: A man knocks someone down and hears them yelp.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal words for a man or boy, as in a decent sort of guy.
